quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with whom
quests.questionSentence: My uncle, whom I haven't seen in years, is visiting next week. Why is 'whom' (not 'who') used here?
quests.targetClause: Because 'my uncle' is the object of 'seen' - 'I' is the subject.
quests.completedSentence: My uncle, whom I haven't seen in years, is visiting next week. Why is 'whom' (not 'who') used here?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'I' is the subject of 'have seen,' making 'my uncle' the object - which calls for 'whom,' regardless of whether the clause is defining or non-defining.
quests.nativeTip: Check who is doing the seeing, and who is being seen.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Because 'my uncle' is the object of 'seen' - 'I' is the subject."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with whom
quests.questionSentence: The keynote speaker, ___ the organizers personally invited, arrived an hour early.
quests.targetClause: whom
quests.completedSentence: The keynote speaker, whom the organizers personally invited, arrived an hour early.
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The organizers' is the subject of 'invited,' making 'the keynote speaker' the object - 'whom' correctly marks this role in a formal, non-defining clause.
quests.nativeTip: Check who is doing the inviting, and who is being invited.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "whom"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with whom
quests.questionSentence: Which of these statements about 'whom' is true?
quests.targetClause: 'Whom' can be used in both defining and non-defining object clauses.
quests.completedSentence: Which of these statements about 'whom' is true?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Whom' marks an object role and works equally well in defining and non-defining clauses - unlike 'that,' which is banned from non-defining clauses entirely.
quests.nativeTip: Think about whether 'whom' cares about commas at all, or only about the grammatical role it plays.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "'Whom' can be used in both defining and non-defining object clauses."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: My colleague, whose office is right next to mine, is out sick today. Is this clause defining or non-defining, and why?
quests.targetClause: Non-defining - 'my colleague' already refers to one specific person, so the office detail is extra.
quests.completedSentence: My colleague, whose office is right next to mine, is out sick today. Is this clause defining or non-defining, and why?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'My colleague' already identifies one specific person, so 'whose office is right next to mine' is extra, non-defining detail, correctly set off with commas.
quests.nativeTip: Think about how many colleagues 'my colleague' could refer to in this sentence - one specific one, or several needing narrowing down?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Non-defining - 'my colleague' already refers to one specific person, so the office detail is extra."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: Which of these sentences is correctly punctuated?
quests.targetClause: Marie Curie, whose research on radioactivity won two Nobel Prizes, remains a scientific icon.
quests.completedSentence: Which of these sentences is correctly punctuated?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'Marie Curie' is a named individual, 'whose research on radioactivity won two Nobel Prizes' is non-defining and needs commas both before and after it.
quests.nativeTip: Marie Curie is a specific, named person - check that the extra detail about her research is set off with commas on both sides.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Marie Curie, whose research on radioactivity won two Nobel Prizes, remains a scientific icon."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Possessive Relative Pronoun whose
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence correctly reflects that there are several employees, and we're identifying one by a specific detail?
quests.targetClause: The employee whose badge was found in the lobby should report to security.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence correctly reflects that there are several employees, and we're identifying one by a specific detail?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since there are multiple employees, 'whose badge was found in the lobby' is essential to identify which one, making this a defining clause with no commas.
quests.nativeTip: Since there are several employees, this detail narrows down which one - check for the correct absence of commas.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The employee whose badge was found in the lobby should report to security."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Adverb of Place (where)
quests.questionSentence: We visited Paris, where we saw the Eiffel Tower. Is 'where we saw the Eiffel Tower' essential to know which city is meant?
quests.targetClause: No - 'Paris' is already a unique, specific city, so this is extra information.
quests.completedSentence: We visited Paris, where we saw the Eiffel Tower. Is 'where we saw the Eiffel Tower' essential to know which city is meant?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'Paris' is already a unique, named place, 'where we saw the Eiffel Tower' is extra, non-defining information about it - correctly set off with a comma, just like non-defining clauses with 'who' or 'which.'
quests.nativeTip: Ask whether 'Paris' needs any narrowing down at all, being a specific, named city.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "No - 'Paris' is already a unique, specific city, so this is extra information."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Adverb of Place (where)
quests.questionSentence: Which of these versions is correctly punctuated?
quests.targetClause: We finally visited Tokyo, where my grandparents were born.
quests.completedSentence: Which of these versions is correctly punctuated?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'Tokyo' is a unique city, 'where my grandparents were born' is non-defining and needs a single comma right before it, since the clause ends the sentence here.
quests.nativeTip: Tokyo is a unique, named city - check that the comma is placed correctly right before the extra detail begins.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "We finally visited Tokyo, where my grandparents were born."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Adverb of Place (where)
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence correctly reflects that the city has several parks, and we're identifying one by a specific detail?
quests.targetClause: The park where the festival takes place every summer is closed for renovations.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence correctly reflects that the city has several parks, and we're identifying one by a specific detail?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since there are multiple parks, 'where the festival takes place every summer' is essential to identify which one, making this a defining clause with no commas.
quests.nativeTip: Since there are several parks, this detail narrows down which one - check for the correct absence of commas.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The park where the festival takes place every summer is closed for renovations."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Adverb of Time (when)
quests.questionSentence: 1969, when humans first landed on the moon, was a landmark year for science. Is 'when humans first landed on the moon' essential to know which year is meant?
quests.targetClause: No - '1969' is already a specific, unique year, so this is extra information.
quests.completedSentence: 1969, when humans first landed on the moon, was a landmark year for science. Is 'when humans first landed on the moon' essential to know which year is meant?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since '1969' is already a specific, unique year, 'when humans first landed on the moon' is extra, non-defining information about it.
quests.nativeTip: Ask whether '1969' needs any narrowing down at all, being a specific, named year.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "No - '1969' is already a specific, unique year, so this is extra information."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Adverb of Time (when)
quests.questionSentence: Which version below is correctly punctuated?
quests.targetClause: Next Friday, when the results are announced, will be a stressful day.
quests.completedSentence: Which version below is correctly punctuated?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'next Friday' is already a specific, unique day, 'when the results are announced' is non-defining and needs commas both before and after it.
quests.nativeTip: 'Next Friday' is already a specific day - check that both commas surrounding this extra detail are present.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Next Friday, when the results are announced, will be a stressful day."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Relative Adverb of Time (when)
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence correctly reflects that there are several possible days, and we're identifying one by a specific detail?
quests.targetClause: The day when the results are announced will be stressful.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence correctly reflects that there are several possible days, and we're identifying one by a specific detail?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'the day' could refer to any day, 'when the results are announced' is essential to identify the specific one, making this a defining clause with no commas.
quests.nativeTip: Since several days are possible, this detail narrows down which one - check for the correct absence of commas.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The day when the results are announced will be stressful."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.grammarRule: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Compare: A) 'The photo I took yesterday is blurry.' B) 'This photo, ___ I took yesterday, is blurry.' Can the blank in sentence B be left empty, the way it was in sentence A?
quests.targetClause: No - non-defining clauses always require their pronoun to stay, even when it's an object relative clause.
quests.completedSentence: Compare: A) 'The photo I took yesterday is blurry.' B) 'This photo, No - non-defining clauses always require their pronoun to stay, even when it's an object relative clause. I took yesterday, is blurry.' Can the blank in sentence B be left empty, the way it was in sentence A?
quests.ruleExplanation: Unlike defining clauses, non-defining clauses can never drop their relative pronoun - doing so would leave the commas dangling with no way to signal where the extra information begins. 'This photo, which I took yesterday, is blurry' must keep 'which.'
quests.nativeTip: Think about what commas signal - could a sentence with commas but no visible pronoun still make sense to a reader?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "No - non-defining clauses always require their pronoun to stay, even when it's an object relative clause."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.grammarRule: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence includes an error?
quests.targetClause: This report, I finished last night, impressed my manager.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence includes an error?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'This report, I finished last night, impressed my manager' incorrectly drops the pronoun inside a non-defining clause - the commas signal extra information, but without 'which,' there's no clear connector; it should read 'This report, which I finished last night, impressed my manager.'
quests.nativeTip: Check each sentence with commas specifically - does the clause between them still have a visible connecting word?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "This report, I finished last night, impressed my manager."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.grammarRule: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: My laptop, ___ I bought just last month, already has a cracked screen.
quests.targetClause: which
quests.completedSentence: My laptop, which I bought just last month, already has a cracked screen.
quests.ruleExplanation: Because this is a non-defining clause (signaled by the commas), the pronoun cannot be omitted; 'which' is required, not 'that' (banned from non-defining clauses) or no word at all.
quests.nativeTip: Notice the commas around this clause - does that change whether the pronoun can be dropped, compared to a defining clause?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "which"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Which Referring to an Entire Clause
quests.grammarRule: Which Referring to an Entire Clause
quests.questionSentence: She apologized, which surprised everyone. What does 'which' refer to in this sentence?
quests.targetClause: The entire idea that she apologized, not just a single noun.
quests.completedSentence: She apologized, which surprised everyone. What does 'which' refer to in this sentence?
quests.ruleExplanation: Unlike most relative clauses, which describe a single noun, this 'which' refers to the entire preceding idea - the fact that she apologized - which is a special, advanced use of non-defining 'which.'
quests.nativeTip: Look for a single noun right before 'which' that it could be describing - is there one, or is it referring to something bigger?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The entire idea that she apologized, not just a single noun."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Which Referring to an Entire Clause
quests.grammarRule: Which Referring to an Entire Clause
quests.questionSentence: He forgot our anniversary, which really hurt my feelings. What does 'which' refer to?
quests.targetClause: The fact that he forgot the anniversary.
quests.completedSentence: He forgot our anniversary, which really hurt my feelings. What does 'which' refer to?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Which' refers to the entire preceding clause - the fact that he forgot the anniversary - not just the word 'anniversary' itself.
quests.nativeTip: Ask what actually 'hurt my feelings' - a specific object, or the whole situation just described?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The fact that he forgot the anniversary."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Which Referring to an Entire Clause
quests.grammarRule: Which Referring to an Entire Clause
quests.questionSentence: Compare: A) 'She lost the necklace, which was a family heirloom.' B) 'She lost the necklace, which upset her deeply.' In which sentence does 'which' refer to the entire idea of losing the necklace, rather than just the necklace itself?
quests.targetClause: Sentence B
quests.completedSentence: Compare: A) 'She lost the necklace, which was a family heirloom.' B) 'She lost the necklace, which upset her deeply.' In which sentence does 'which' refer to the entire idea of losing the necklace, rather than just the necklace itself?
quests.ruleExplanation: In sentence A, 'which' refers to 'the necklace' specifically - the necklace was the heirloom. In sentence B, 'which' refers to the entire event of losing the necklace - the losing is what upset her, not the necklace itself.
quests.nativeTip: Ask what was actually 'a family heirloom' versus what actually 'upset her deeply' - a single object, or the whole event?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Sentence B"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: The manager who approved the budget, which had been under review for months, finally announced the decision. Which clause is defining, and which is non-defining?
quests.targetClause: 'who approved the budget' is defining; 'which had been under review for months' is non-defining.
quests.completedSentence: The manager who approved the budget, which had been under review for months, finally announced the decision. Which clause is defining, and which is non-defining?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who approved the budget' has no commas and identifies which manager - defining. 'Which had been under review for months,' set off by a comma, adds extra detail about the budget - non-defining.
quests.nativeTip: Check the punctuation around each clause separately - one has commas, one doesn't.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "'who approved the budget' is defining; 'which had been under review for months' is non-defining."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is correctly punctuated, given that there are several interns but only one CEO?
quests.targetClause: The intern who impressed the CEO, who founded the company in 2010, got a full-time offer.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is correctly punctuated, given that there are several interns but only one CEO?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'Who impressed the CEO' is defining, since there are several interns and no commas are used; 'who founded the company in 2010' is non-defining, since there's one CEO and it needs commas.
quests.nativeTip: Check each clause against its antecedent separately - 'intern' has several candidates, 'CEO' has only one.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The intern who impressed the CEO, who founded the company in 2010, got a full-time offer."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence is correctly punctuated, given that the museum has several galleries but only one director?
quests.targetClause: The gallery that features modern art, which the director personally redesigned last year, is the most popular.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence is correctly punctuated, given that the museum has several galleries but only one director?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'That features modern art' is defining, since there are several galleries, so no commas and 'that' is fine; 'which the director personally redesigned last year' is non-defining, since there's one director, so it needs commas and must use 'which,' not 'that.'
quests.nativeTip: Check each clause against its antecedent separately - 'gallery' has several candidates, 'director' has only one.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The gallery that features modern art, which the director personally redesigned last year, is the most popular."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Comma Placement in Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Fix this sentence: 'My father who taught me to drive, always says patience is key.' The speaker has only one father.
quests.targetClause: My father, who taught me to drive, always says patience is key.
quests.completedSentence: Fix this sentence: 'My father who taught me to drive, always says patience is key.' The speaker has only one father.
quests.ruleExplanation: The original sentence was missing the opening comma; the fix adds a comma both before and after 'who taught me to drive,' since this is non-defining information about a uniquely identified person.
quests.nativeTip: Since there's only one father, both commas need to be added correctly around the extra detail - check where exactly they belong.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "My father, who taught me to drive, always says patience is key."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: That Cannot Introduce Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Fix this sentence: 'The suitcase, that was left at the gate, needs to be identified.' There are multiple suitcases at the gate.
quests.targetClause: The suitcase that was left at the gate needs to be identified.
quests.completedSentence: Fix this sentence: 'The suitcase, that was left at the gate, needs to be identified.' There are multiple suitcases at the gate.
quests.ruleExplanation: The original sentence wrongly used commas, implying only one suitcase, and 'that' after a comma, which is never allowed. The fix removes both commas entirely, since this is a defining clause identifying which suitcase among several.
quests.nativeTip: Since there are multiple suitcases, all commas need to be removed, and 'that' should stay since it's fine in defining clauses.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "The suitcase that was left at the gate needs to be identified."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: That Cannot Introduce Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Fix this sentence: 'The bridge, that was built in 1932, connects the two districts.' There is only one such bridge.
quests.targetClause: The bridge, which was built in 1932, connects the two districts.
quests.completedSentence: Fix this sentence: 'The bridge, that was built in 1932, connects the two districts.' There is only one such bridge.
quests.ruleExplanation: The commas were already correct for this non-defining clause, but 'that' is never allowed after a comma; simply swapping in 'which' fixes the sentence.
quests.nativeTip: The commas are already correctly placed - only the pronoun itself needs to change.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "The bridge, which was built in 1932, connects the two districts."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Comma Placement in Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: The vaccine, which underwent years of testing, was finally approved for public use. Is this sentence correctly punctuated, assuming there is only one vaccine being discussed?
quests.targetClause: Yes, it's correctly punctuated
quests.completedSentence: The vaccine, which underwent years of testing, was finally approved for public use. Is this sentence correctly punctuated, assuming there is only one vaccine being discussed?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since there's only one vaccine being discussed, 'which underwent years of testing' is non-defining extra information, and both the comma before and after it are correctly placed.
quests.nativeTip: Check whether both a person/thing is uniquely identified and both commas are present around the extra detail.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Yes, it's correctly punctuated"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Object Relative Clause with whom
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence about a specific named author is correctly punctuated?
quests.targetClause: Toni Morrison, whom critics widely admired, won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence about a specific named author is correctly punctuated?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since 'Toni Morrison' is a specific, named person, 'whom critics widely admired' is non-defining and needs commas both before and after it.
quests.nativeTip: A named author is already uniquely identified - check that the extra detail about critical reception is set off with commas on both sides.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Toni Morrison, whom critics widely admired, won the Nobel Prize in Literature."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Antecedent Identification
quests.questionSentence: The proposal from our newest hire, which impressed the entire board, will be implemented next quarter. What does 'which impressed the entire board' actually describe?
quests.targetClause: the proposal
quests.completedSentence: The proposal from our newest hire, which impressed the entire board, will be implemented next quarter. What does 'which impressed the entire board' actually describe?
quests.ruleExplanation: 'The proposal' - not 'our newest hire' - is what impressed the board; the comma confirms this is extra, non-defining detail about a specific, already-identified proposal.
quests.nativeTip: 'From our newest hire' just tells you the source - check what actually impressed the board.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "the proposal"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: That Cannot Introduce Non-Defining Clauses
quests.questionSentence: Which sentence about a company's single flagship product is grammatically and logically correct?
quests.targetClause: Our flagship product, which revolutionized the industry, remains our top seller.
quests.completedSentence: Which sentence about a company's single flagship product is grammatically and logically correct?
quests.ruleExplanation: Since there's only one flagship product, this clause is non-defining and needs commas on both sides; 'which' - not 'that' - must introduce it, since 'that' can never follow a comma.
quests.nativeTip: Check three things: is the pronoun allowed after a comma, are both commas present, and does the punctuation match the fact there's only one such product?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "Our flagship product, which revolutionized the industry, remains our top seller."

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.grammarRule: Non-Defining Clauses Cannot Omit Their Pronoun
quests.questionSentence: This contract, ___ our legal team reviewed for weeks, is finally ready to sign.
quests.targetClause: which
quests.completedSentence: This contract, which our legal team reviewed for weeks, is finally ready to sign.
quests.ruleExplanation: Even though 'our legal team reviewed' makes this an object relative clause, which could normally be omitted, the commas signal a non-defining clause - and non-defining clauses can never drop their pronoun, nor can they use 'that.' 'Which' is the only correct choice.
quests.nativeTip: Notice the commas - does that change whether this pronoun could ever be dropped, even though it's technically an object relative clause?
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [non-defining] ➔ "which"

quests.conceptTitle: Information Snap-In: Defining vs Non-Defining Relative Clause
quests.questionSentence: Compare: A) 'The witnesses who testified consistently were believed by the jury.' B) 'The witnesses, who testified consistently, were believed by the jury.' Which sentence implies that some witnesses did NOT testify consistently?
quests.targetClause: Sentence A
quests.completedSentence: Compare: A) 'The witnesses who testified consistently were believed by the jury.' B) 'The witnesses, who testified consistently, were believed by the jury.' Which sentence implies that some witnesses did NOT testify consistently?
quests.ruleExplanation: Sentence A, with no commas, implies that only some witnesses testified consistently - the clause distinguishes them from others who may not have. Sentence B implies all the witnesses being discussed testified consistently, since the clause is just extra, non-defining information about the whole group.
quests.nativeTip: Ask whether the clause is narrowing down a specific group of witnesses, or describing a fact true of every witness already mentioned.
quests.legoPreview: 🧩 Snap Slot: [defining] ➔ "Sentence A"
